claim: C. elegans produces ascaroside pheromones to control its development and behavior.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans produces ascaroside pheromones to control its development and behavior.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by multiple citations in the introduction section.

claim: Minor structural differences in the ascarosides have dramatic consequences for their biological activities.
source: Even minor structural differences in the ascarosides have dramatic consequences for their biological activities.
evidence: This is supported by examples provided in the introduction showing different biological activities of structurally similar ascarosides.

claim: C. elegans uses the peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase ACS-7 to activate the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides for β-oxidation in response to starvation.
source: In response to starvation, C. elegans uses the peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetase ACS-7 to activate the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides for β-oxidation involving the acyl-CoA oxidases ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by enzymatic assays, mutant analysis, and localization studies presented in the results section.

claim: The β-oxidation pathway involving ACS-7, ACOX-1.1, and ACOX-3 rapidly converts a favorable ascaroside pheromone that induces aggregation to an unfavorable one that induces the stress-resistant dauer larval stage.
source: This pathway rapidly converts a favorable ascaroside pheromone that induces aggregation to an unfavorable one that induces the stress-resistant dauer larval stage.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing conversion of IC-asc-C9 (aggregation pheromone) to IC-asc-C5 (dauer pheromone) through the identified pathway.

claim: The pathway allows C. elegans to respond to changing environmental conditions and alter its chemical message without having to synthesize new ascarosides de novo.
source: Thus, the pathway allows the worm to respond to changing environmental conditions and alter its chemical message without having to synthesize new ascarosides de novo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by the demonstration that existing IC-ascarosides can be modified through β-oxidation.

claim: Side-chain β-oxidation is critical for controlling the type of IC-ascarosides produced.
source: We establish a new model for biosynthesis of the IC-ascarosides in which side-chain β-oxidation is critical for controlling the type of IC-ascarosides produced.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that β-oxidation of IC-ascarosides determines their final side-chain length and biological activity.

claim: Ascarosides induce development of the dauer larval stage at high population densities.
source: The nematode C. elegans secretes ascarosides as pheromones to induce development of the dauer larval stage at high population densities, as well as to control various behaviors, including male attraction to hermaphrodites, hermaphrodite attraction to males, avoidance, foraging behavior, and adult aggregation (Cassada and Russell, 1975; Golden and Riddle, 1982; Butcher et al., 2007; Butcher et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2008; Butcher et al., 2009a; Pungaliya et al., 2009; Izrayelit et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Artyukhin et al., 2013; Greene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Ascarosides control various behaviors in C. elegans, including male attraction to hermaphrodites, hermaphrodite attraction to males, avoidance, foraging behavior, and adult aggregation.
source: The nematode C. elegans secretes ascarosides as pheromones to induce development of the dauer larval stage at high population densities, as well as to control various behaviors, including male attraction to hermaphrodites, hermaphrodite attraction to males, avoidance, foraging behavior, and adult aggregation (Cassada and Russell, 1975; Golden and Riddle, 1982; Butcher et al., 2007; Butcher et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2008; Butcher et al., 2009a; Pungaliya et al., 2009; Izrayelit et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Artyukhin et al., 2013; Greene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Ascarosides are derivatives of the 3,6-dideoxysugar ascarylose.
source: The ascarosides are derivatives of the 3,6-dideoxysugar ascarylose that can be named according to their structural features, including the number of carbons (C#) in their fatty acid-derived side chains (Butcher, 2017).
evidence: This is a structural definition supported by citation.

claim: Ascaroside side chains are attached to the ascarylose sugar at their penultimate (ω−1) or terminal (ω) carbon.
source: These side chains are attached to the ascarylose sugar at their penultimate (ω−1) or terminal (ω) carbon and are often unsaturated (Δ) at the α-β position.
evidence: This is a structural description of ascarosides.

claim: Ascaroside side chains are often unsaturated (Δ) at the α-β position.
source: These side chains are attached to the ascarylose sugar at their penultimate (ω−1) or terminal (ω) carbon and are often unsaturated (Δ) at the α-β position.
evidence: This is a structural description of ascarosides.

claim: Ascarosides can be modified with various head groups at the 4'-position of the ascarylose sugar, such as the IC, OS, HB, and MB groups.
source: The ascarosides can be modified with various head groups at the 4'-position of the ascarylose sugar, such as the IC, the octopamine succinyl (OS), the 4-hydroxybenzoyl (HB), and the (E)-2-methyl-2-butenoyl (MB) groups.
evidence: This is a structural description of ascaroside modifications.

claim: Ascarosides can be modified with various terminus groups at the end of their fatty-acid side chain.
source: They can also be modified with various terminus groups at the end of their fatty-acid side chain.
evidence: This is a structural description of ascaroside modifications.

claim: Head and terminus modifications can have important consequences for the biological activity of the ascarosides.
source: These head and terminus modifications can have important consequences for the biological activity of the ascarosides.
evidence: This is supported by examples provided in the text showing different biological activities.

claim: Unmodified, simple ascarosides are often negative signals that induce avoidance in C. elegans.
source: For example, while unmodified, simple ascarosides are often negative signals that induce avoidance in C. elegans, ascarosides that are modified with an IC head group, such as IC-asc-ΔC9 (icas#3), are favorable signals that induce aggregation at picomolar concentrations (Srinivasan et al., 2012; von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IC-asc-ΔC9 (icas#3) is a favorable signal that induces aggregation at picomolar concentrations.
source: For example, while unmodified, simple ascarosides are often negative signals that induce avoidance in C. elegans, ascarosides that are modified with an IC head group, such as IC-asc-ΔC9 (icas#3), are favorable signals that induce aggregation at picomolar concentrations (Srinivasan et al., 2012; von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IC-asc-C5 (icas#9) is one of the five primary components of the dauer pheromone.
source: For example, unlike IC-ascarosides with medium-length (C9) side chains, which do not induce dauer, an IC-ascaroside with a short (C5) side chain, IC-asc-C5 (icas#9), is one of the five primary components of the dauer pheromone and induces the dauer larval stage when it accumulates at low nanomolar concentrations (Butcher et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IC-asc-C5 induces the dauer larval stage when it accumulates at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: For example, unlike IC-ascarosides with medium-length (C9) side chains, which do not induce dauer, an IC-ascaroside with a short (C5) side chain, IC-asc-C5 (icas#9), is one of the five primary components of the dauer pheromone and induces the dauer larval stage when it accumulates at low nanomolar concentrations (Butcher et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IC-ascarosides with medium-length (C9) side chains do not induce dauer.
source: For example, unlike IC-ascarosides with medium-length (C9) side chains, which do not induce dauer, an IC-ascaroside with a short (C5) side chain, IC-asc-C5 (icas#9), is one of the five primary components of the dauer pheromone and induces the dauer larval stage when it accumulates at low nanomolar concentrations (Butcher et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: IC-ascarosides have a dual nature to their activity as they are generally favorable signals that induce aggregation on food, but can also indicate unfavorable conditions and induce dauer when they have short side chains and accumulate to higher concentrations.
source: Thus, IC-ascarosides have a dual nature to their activity as they are generally favorable signals that induce aggregation on food, but can also indicate unfavorable conditions and induce dauer when they have short side chains and accumulate to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the biological activities described in the text.

claim: Peroxisomal β-oxidation is central to biosynthesis of the ascarosides.
source: Peroxisomal β-oxidation is central to biosynthesis of the ascarosides.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: β-oxidation cycles shorten the side chains of long-chain ascaroside precursors by two carbons per cycle to produce short- and medium-chain ascaroside pheromones.
source: β-oxidation cycles shorten the side chains of long-chain ascaroside precursors by two carbons per cycle to produce short- and medium-chain ascaroside pheromones (Golden and Riddle, 1985; Wanders and Waterham, 2006; Butcher et al., 2009b; Joo et al., 2009; Joo et al., 2010; von Reuss et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The first step in β-oxidation cycles is catalyzed by an acyl-CoA oxidase, which installs a double bond at the α-β position of its substrate in a reaction that uses an FAD cofactor and produces H2O2.
source: The first step in these β-oxidation cycles is catalyzed by an acyl-CoA oxidase, which installs a double bond at the α-β position of its substrate in a reaction that uses an FAD cofactor and produces H2O2.
evidence: This is a description of the enzymatic mechanism of acyl-CoA oxidases.

claim: Specific acyl-CoA oxidases process ascaroside precursors with specific side-chain lengths and thus help to control which pheromones are produced.
source: Specific acyl-CoA oxidases process ascaroside precursors with specific side-chain lengths and thus help to control which pheromones are produced (Joo et al., 2010; von Reuss et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The C. elegans genome encodes seven acyl-CoA oxidases.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes seven acyl-CoA oxidases, five of which have been implicated in ascaroside production (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Five acyl-CoA oxidases have been implicated in ascaroside production.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes seven acyl-CoA oxidases, five of which have been implicated in ascaroside production (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The remaining three steps in each β-oxidation cycle are catalyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase (MAOC-1), an (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (DHS-28), and a 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (DAF-22).
source: The remaining three steps in each β-oxidation cycle are catalyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase (MAOC-1), an (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (DHS-28), and a 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (DAF-22) (Butcher et al., 2009b; Joo et al., 2009; Joo et al., 2010; von Reuss et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: (ω−1)-ascarosides and ω-ascarosides are biosynthesized by two parallel β-oxidation pathways.
source: Our group has shown that (ω−1)-ascarosides and ω-ascarosides are biosynthesized by two parallel β-oxidation pathways, the former pathway involving ACOX-1.1, ACOX-1.3, ACOX-1.4, and ACOX-3 and the latter pathway involving ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-1.2 (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: The (ω−1)-ascaroside biosynthetic pathway involves ACOX-1.1, ACOX-1.3, ACOX-1.4, and ACOX-3.
source: Our group has shown that (ω−1)-ascarosides and ω-ascarosides are biosynthesized by two parallel β-oxidation pathways, the former pathway involving ACOX-1.1, ACOX-1.3, ACOX-1.4, and ACOX-3 and the latter pathway involving ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-1.2 (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: The ω-ascaroside biosynthetic pathway involves ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-1.2.
source: Our group has shown that (ω−1)-ascarosides and ω-ascarosides are biosynthesized by two parallel β-oxidation pathways, the former pathway involving ACOX-1.1, ACOX-1.3, ACOX-1.4, and ACOX-3 and the latter pathway involving ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-1.2 (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Extensive β-oxidation of ascaroside precursors to make ascarosides with very short side chains generates some of the most potent dauer pheromones, such as asc-ωC3 (ascr#5).
source: In general, extensive β-oxidation of ascaroside precursors by these pathways to make ascarosides with very short side chains generates some of the most potent dauer pheromones, such as asc-ωC3 (ascr#5).
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between side-chain length and dauer-inducing activity.

claim: Very little is known about how various head groups, such as the IC, OS, HB, and MB groups, become attached to the ascarosides.
source: Very little is known about how various head groups, such as the IC, OS, HB, and MB groups, become attached to the ascarosides and how this attachment process is coordinated with the β-oxidation process that shortens the ascaroside side chains.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Very little is known about how the attachment of head groups is coordinated with the β-oxidation process that shortens the ascaroside side chains.
source: Very little is known about how various head groups, such as the IC, OS, HB, and MB groups, become attached to the ascarosides and how this attachment process is coordinated with the β-oxidation process that shortens the ascaroside side chains.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Attachment of the IC head group to the 4'-position of the ascarylose is thought to occur late in the biosynthetic pathway after β-oxidation of the side chain has occurred.
source: Attachment of the IC head group to the 4'-position of the ascarylose is thought to occur late in the biosynthetic pathway after β-oxidation of the side chain has occurred (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a previous hypothesis supported by citation, which the current study challenges.

claim: Exogenous addition of synthetic asc-C9 (ascr#10) to daf-22 worms leads to production of IC-asc-C9 (icas#10).
source: The exogenous addition of a synthetic ascaroside with a nine-carbon side chain, asc-C9 (ascr#10), to daf-22 worms (which are defective in β-oxidation and thus cannot make short- and medium-chain ascarosides, but which presumably can still biosynthesize the IC group and attach it) leads to production of the corresponding IC-ascaroside, IC-asc-C9 (icas#10) (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: daf-22 worms are defective in β-oxidation and thus cannot make short- and medium-chain ascarosides.
source: The exogenous addition of a synthetic ascaroside with a nine-carbon side chain, asc-C9 (ascr#10), to daf-22 worms (which are defective in β-oxidation and thus cannot make short- and medium-chain ascarosides, but which presumably can still biosynthesize the IC group and attach it) leads to production of the corresponding IC-ascaroside, IC-asc-C9 (icas#10) (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of daf-22 mutants.

claim: The acyl-CoA synthetase gene acs-7 is required for biosynthesis of the short-chain IC- and OS-modified ascarosides, IC-asc-C5 and OS-asc-C5 (osas#9).
source: The acyl-CoA synthetase gene, acs-7, has been shown to be required for biosynthesis of the short-chain IC- and OS-modified ascarosides, IC-asc-C5 and OS-asc-C5 (osas#9), but not for medium-chain IC- and OS-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9 and OS-asc-C9 (osas#10) (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: acs-7 is not required for biosynthesis of medium-chain IC- and OS-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9 and OS-asc-C9 (osas#10).
source: The acyl-CoA synthetase gene, acs-7, has been shown to be required for biosynthesis of the short-chain IC- and OS-modified ascarosides, IC-asc-C5 and OS-asc-C5 (osas#9), but not for medium-chain IC- and OS-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9 and OS-asc-C9 (osas#10) (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Panda et al. proposed that ACS-7 activates indole-3-carboxylic acid (ICA) as the corresponding CoA-thioester (IC-CoA) and is involved in the attachment of the IC group specifically to the short-chain ascaroside asc-C5 (ascr#9) to make IC-asc-C5.
source: Panda et al. proposed that ACS-7 activates indole-3-carboxylic acid (ICA) as the corresponding CoA-thioester (IC-CoA) and is involved in the attachment of the IC group specifically to the short-chain ascaroside asc-C5 (ascr#9) to make IC-asc-C5 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of a previous hypothesis, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Panda et al. were able to show that ACS-7 activates ICA as an AMP-ester (IC-AMP).
source: However, while Panda et al. were able to show that ACS-7 activates ICA as an AMP-ester (IC-AMP), they could not show that ACS-7 catalyzes the formation of IC-CoA or attachment of the IC group to an ascaroside (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental results, supported by citation.

claim: Panda et al. could not show that ACS-7 catalyzes the formation of IC-CoA or attachment of the IC group to an ascaroside.
source: However, while Panda et al. were able to show that ACS-7 activates ICA as an AMP-ester (IC-AMP), they could not show that ACS-7 catalyzes the formation of IC-CoA or attachment of the IC group to an ascaroside (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of limitations in previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Panda et al. interpreted their data to mean that some other protein or factor was required for the full activity of ACS-7.
source: Their interpretation of these data was that some other protein or factor was required for the full activity of ACS-7.
evidence: This is a description of the interpretation made by previous researchers.

claim: Mutant worms lacking lysosome-related organelles (LROs) do not make 4'-modified ascarosides.
source: Panda et al. showed that mutant worms lacking lysosome-related organelles (LROs) did not make 4'-modified ascarosides, and they reported that ACS-7 was expressed in the lysosome (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Panda et al. reported that ACS-7 was expressed in the lysosome.
source: Panda et al. showed that mutant worms lacking lysosome-related organelles (LROs) did not make 4'-modified ascarosides, and they reported that ACS-7 was expressed in the lysosome (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a previous finding that the current study contradicts, supported by citation.

claim: Panda et al. concluded that ACS-7 was functioning inside the lysosomes in IC-ascaroside biosynthesis.
source: Thus, they concluded that ACS-7 was functioning inside the lysosomes in IC-ascaroside biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a description of the conclusion from previous work, which the current study challenges.

claim: The role of ACS-7 is to activate the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides for shortening through β-oxidation.
source: Here, we show that the role of the acyl-CoA synthetase ACS-7 is not to attach the IC group to ascarosides as proposed by Panda et al., but to activate the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides for shortening through β-oxidation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: β-oxidation of the side chain occurs after attachment of the IC head group in the biosynthesis of the short-chain IC-ascarosides.
source: Thus, in contrast to the previously proposed model, we show that β-oxidation of the side chain occurs after attachment of the IC head group in the biosynthesis of the short-chain IC-ascarosides.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study that contradicts the previous model.

claim: Production of aggregation pheromones likely occurs under favorable environmental conditions such as food-rich conditions as C. elegans tends to aggregate on food.
source: Production of aggregation pheromones likely occurs under favorable environmental conditions such as food-rich conditions as C. elegans tends to aggregate on food (Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological behavior of C. elegans, supported by citation.

claim: If conditions decline, such as during starvation, the side chains of IC-ascarosides can be activated by ACS-7 and then shortened through peroxisomal β-oxidation cycles involving ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 to make the potent dauer pheromone IC-asc-C5.
source: However, if conditions decline, such as during starvation, the side chains of these IC-ascarosides can be activated by ACS-7 and then shortened through peroxisomal β-oxidation cycles involving ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 to make the potent dauer pheromone IC-asc-C5.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by enzymatic assays and mutant analysis.

claim: ACS-7 is localized to the peroxisome.
source: Consistent with its function in activating ascarosides for peroxisomal β-oxidation, ACS-7 is localized to the peroxisome, rather than the lysosome, as previously reported by Panda et al.
evidence: This is supported by the localization data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The mechanism by which C. elegans converts aggregation-inducing, medium-chain IC-ascarosides to dauer-inducing, short-chain IC-ascarosides involves ACS-7, ACOX-1.1, and ACOX-3.
source: Our results uncover the mechanism by which C. elegans responds to declining environmental conditions and converts aggregation-inducing, medium-chain IC-ascarosides to dauer-inducing, short-chain IC-ascarosides.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: This mechanism is likely also used by C. elegans in the biosynthesis of short-chain OS-ascarosides, which induce nematode dispersal under unfavorable conditions.
source: This mechanism is likely also used by C. elegans in the biosynthesis of short-chain OS-ascarosides, which induce nematode dispersal under unfavorable conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between IC- and OS-ascaroside biosynthesis.

claim: Using this mechanism, C. elegans can efficiently alter the function of existing ascarosides simply by tailoring the length of the side chain.
source: Using this mechanism, C. elegans can efficiently alter the function of existing ascarosides simply by tailoring the length of the side chain, providing a novel strategy to rapidly modulate chemical signaling in response to environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: daf-22 worms can attach the IC group to exogenously provided asc-ΔC9 (ascr#3) to produce IC-asc-ΔC9.
source: It was also shown that daf-22 worms can attach the IC group to exogenously provided asc-ΔC9 (ascr#3) to produce IC-asc-ΔC9 (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The unknown enzyme that attaches the IC group specifically prefers ascarosides with side chains of 8–11 carbons in length.
source: These data suggest that the unknown enzyme that attaches the IC group specifically prefers ascarosides with side chains of 8–11 carbons in length (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C. elegans does not preferentially attach the IC group to ascarosides with C5 or C7 side chains.
source: Thus, we conclude that C. elegans does not preferentially attach the IC group to ascarosides with C5 or C7 side chains.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing very low conversion of asc-C5 and asc-C7 to their IC-modified forms.

claim: Short chain IC-ascarosides, IC-asc-C5 and IC-asc-C7, could potentially be made from medium-chain IC-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9, which have their side chains shortened through β-oxidation.
source: Therefore, we speculated that these short chain IC-ascarosides could potentially be made from medium-chain IC-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9, which have their side chains shortened through β-oxidation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that C. elegans can make short-chain IC-ascarosides but does not preferentially attach the IC group to short-chain ascarosides.

claim: The KM of ACS-7 for ICA (in the one-step reaction to produce IC-AMP) is 270 ± 90 μM.
source: Furthermore, the KM of ACS-7 for ICA (in the one-step reaction to produce IC-AMP) is 270 ± 90 μM (Panda et al., 2017), which is much higher than the KM values of acyl-CoA synthetases from other organisms (in the two-step reaction to produce an acyl-CoA) that are generally in the low μM range (Hall et al., 2003; Van Horn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a kinetic parameter from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The KM of ACS-7 for ICA is much higher than the KM values of acyl-CoA synthetases from other organisms that are generally in the low μM range.
source: Furthermore, the KM of ACS-7 for ICA (in the one-step reaction to produce IC-AMP) is 270 ± 90 μM (Panda et al., 2017), which is much higher than the KM values of acyl-CoA synthetases from other organisms (in the two-step reaction to produce an acyl-CoA) that are generally in the low μM range (Hall et al., 2003; Van Horn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison with known kinetic parameters from other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: The acs-7 mutant accumulates IC-asc-C9, while failing to make IC-asc-C5.
source: The acs-7 mutant accumulates IC-asc-C9, while failing to make IC-asc-C5 (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a phenotype of the acs-7 mutant, supported by citation.

claim: ACS-7 showed robust activity towards IC-asc-C9, rapidly converting it completely to the corresponding CoA-thioester within 10 min.
source: ACS-7 showed robust activity towards this substrate, rapidly converting it completely to the corresponding CoA-thioester within 10 min (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ACS-7(E339A) single mutant showed very little activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate.
source: The ACS-7(E339A) single mutant showed very little activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate, and the ACS-7(E339A, S186A, S187A) triple mutant showed no activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate, thereby confirming that the activity seen for the wild-type enzyme does not result from any copurifying proteins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ACS-7(E339A, S186A, S187A) triple mutant showed no activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate.
source: The ACS-7(E339A) single mutant showed very little activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate, and the ACS-7(E339A, S186A, S187A) triple mutant showed no activity towards the IC-asc-C9 substrate, thereby confirming that the activity seen for the wild-type enzyme does not result from any copurifying proteins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ACS-7 showed very little activity towards ICA.
source: ACS-7 showed very little activity towards ICA, the putative substrate reported by Panda et al.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: During the reaction of ACS-7 with ICA, accumulation of the AMP-ester intermediate was observed, suggesting that ACS-7 is very sluggish towards the ICA substrate and does not turn it over to the corresponding CoA-thioester.
source: During the reaction of ACS-7 with ICA, we saw accumulation of the AMP-ester intermediate, suggesting that ACS-7 is very sluggish towards the ICA substrate and does not turn it over to the corresponding CoA-thioester (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reaction of ACS-7 with ICA to produce the corresponding CoA-thioester required a 2-hour incubation.
source: Although we were able to detect the conversion of ICA to the corresponding CoA-thioester, the reaction required a 2-hour incubation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: More than 60% of the ICA substrate remained as the AMP-ester after 2 hours of incubation with ACS-7.
source: Furthermore, based on the UV absorption at 280 nm, more than 60% of the substrate remained as the AMP-ester at this late time point.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: ACS-7 strongly prefers IC-modified ascarosides over simple ascarosides.
source: These data show that ACS-7 strongly prefers IC-modified ascarosides over simple ascarosides, demonstrating that it is specifically involved in activation of IC-modified ascarosides for β-oxidation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ACS-7 activates the longer-chain substrates (IC-asc-C7 and IC-asc-C9), but not short-chain substrates (IC-asc-C5).
source: ACS-7 activates the longer-chain substrates (IC-asc-C7 and IC-asc-C9), but not short-chain substrates (IC-asc-C5), consistent with its role in shortening the longer-chain substrates.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ACS-7 can activate fatty acids with medium-length side chains, but not short side chains.
source: ACS-7 can activate fatty acids with medium-length side chains, but not short side chains.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The KM of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 14.5 ± 3.0 μM.
source: The KM of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 14.5 ± 3.0 μM, the kcat is 0.53 ± 0.08 s−1, and the kcat/KM is 36,300 ± 9,200 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is a kinetic parameter determined experimentally in this study.

claim: The kcat of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 0.53 ± 0.08 s−1.
source: The KM of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 14.5 ± 3.0 μM, the kcat is 0.53 ± 0.08 s−1, and the kcat/KM is 36,300 ± 9,200 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is a kinetic parameter determined experimentally in this study.

claim: The kcat/KM of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 36,300 ± 9,200 M−1 s−1.
source: The KM of ACS-7 for IC-asc-C9 is 14.5 ± 3.0 μM, the kcat is 0.53 ± 0.08 s−1, and the kcat/KM is 36,300 ± 9,200 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is a kinetic parameter determined experimentally in this study.

claim: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 work together in the β-oxidation cycles that shorten ascarosides with 15-carbon and 13-carbon side chains.
source: We have shown that ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 work together in the β-oxidation cycles that shorten ascarosides with 15-carbon and 13-carbon side chains (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 play a role in biosynthesis of short-chain IC-ascarosides.
source: Analysis of the ascarosides produced by acox-1.1 and acox-3 mutant worms indicates that these acyl-CoA oxidases also play a role in biosynthesis of short-chain IC-ascarosides.
evidence: This is supported by the mutant analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Production of ascarosides and corresponding IC-ascarosides does not always correlate.
source: The amounts of the ascarosides and corresponding IC-ascarosides in wild-type, acox-1.1, acox-3, and acox-1.1;acox-3 worms suggest that production of these two groups of ascarosides does not always correlate (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: It is unlikely that the IC group is directly added to short-chain ascarosides to make the corresponding IC-ascarosides.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that the IC group is directly added to short-chain ascarosides to make the corresponding IC-ascarosides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ascaroside and IC-ascaroside production do not correlate.

claim: The acox-1.1(ok2257) deletion mutant shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7.
source: The acox-1.1(ok2257) deletion mutant shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7, indicating that ACOX-1.1 may function in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens a seven-carbon IC-ascaroside to a five-carbon IC-ascaroside (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACOX-1.1 may function in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens a seven-carbon IC-ascaroside to a five-carbon IC-ascaroside.
source: The acox-1.1(ok2257) deletion mutant shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7, indicating that ACOX-1.1 may function in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens a seven-carbon IC-ascaroside to a five-carbon IC-ascaroside (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation of IC-asc-C7 in the mutant.

claim: The acox-3(tm4033) deletion mutant shows decreased production of IC-asc-C5, but increased accumulation of IC-asc-C7 and IC-asc-ΔC9.
source: The acox-3(tm4033) deletion mutant shows decreased production of IC-asc-C5, but increased accumulation of IC-asc-C7 and IC-asc-ΔC9 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOX-3 may function in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens a seven-carbon IC-ascaroside to a five-carbon IC-ascaroside.
source: Thus, like ACOX-1.1, ACOX-3 may function in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens a seven-carbon IC-ascaroside to a five-carbon IC-ascaroside.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the acox-3 mutant.

claim: The acox-1.1(ok2257);acox-3(tm4033) double deletion mutant completely abolishes production of IC-asc-C5.
source: The ascaroside profile of the acox-1.1(ok2257);acox-3(tm4033) double deletion mutant is quite striking in that production of IC-asc-C5 is completely abolished, while the amount of IC-asc-C7 is increased relative to wild type (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The acox-1.1(ok2257);acox-3(tm4033) double deletion mutant shows increased amount of IC-asc-C7 relative to wild type.
source: The ascaroside profile of the acox-1.1(ok2257);acox-3(tm4033) double deletion mutant is quite striking in that production of IC-asc-C5 is completely abolished, while the amount of IC-asc-C7 is increased relative to wild type (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The amount of IC-asc-C7 is increased in the acox-1.1;acox-3 double mutant despite the amount of asc-C7 being decreased.
source: The amount of IC-asc-C7 is increased despite the amount of asc-C7 being decreased, indicating that production of the ascarosides and IC-ascarosides are independently regulated.
evidence: This is an observation from the data that supports independent regulation of ascarosides and IC-ascarosides.

claim: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 participate in a β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C7 to IC-asc-C5.
source: These data thus provide further evidence that ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 participate in a β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C7 to IC-asc-C5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutant analysis data.

claim: The acox-1.1(reb2[E434A]) catalytic mutant strain shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7.
source: This strain shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7, indicating that ACOX-1.1's catalytic activity contributes to the shortening of IC-ascarosides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOX-1.1's catalytic activity contributes to the shortening of IC-ascarosides.
source: This strain shows an accumulation of IC-asc-C7, indicating that ACOX-1.1's catalytic activity contributes to the shortening of IC-ascarosides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the catalytic mutant.

claim: ACOX-1.4 may contribute to the β-oxidation of IC-ascarosides.
source: In addition to ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3, ACOX-1.4 may also contribute to the β-oxidation of IC-ascarosides.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of multiple mutant strains.

claim: The acox-1.1(reb2[E434A]);acox-1.4(reb6[E433A]);acox-3(tm4033) triple mutant shows that all three genes contribute to the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C9 to IC-asc-C7.
source: However, examination of the acox-1.1(reb2[E434A]);acox-1.4(reb6[E433A]);acox-3(tm4033) triple mutant shows that all three genes contribute to the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C9 to IC-asc-C7, as well as the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C7 to IC-asc-C5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOX-1.1, ACOX-1.4, and ACOX-3 contribute to the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C7 to IC-asc-C5.
source: However, examination of the acox-1.1(reb2[E434A]);acox-1.4(reb6[E433A]);acox-3(tm4033) triple mutant shows that all three genes contribute to the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C9 to IC-asc-C7, as well as the β-oxidation cycle that shortens IC-asc-C7 to IC-asc-C5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 both enabled the conversion of IC-asc-C9-CoA to IC-asc-C5-CoA in vitro.
source: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 both enabled the conversion of IC-asc-C9-CoA to IC-asc-C5-CoA.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACOX-1.2 was inactive in the assay with IC-asc-C9-CoA.
source: On the other hand, ACOX-1.2, which has a small active site and strictly prefers short-chain substrates (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016), was inactive in this assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: ACOX-1.2 has a small active site and strictly prefers short-chain substrates.
source: On the other hand, ACOX-1.2, which has a small active site and strictly prefers short-chain substrates (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016), was inactive in this assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 reactions, IC-asc-C9-CoA was converted to IC-asc-C5-CoA, which was partially hydrolyzed to IC-asc-C5.
source: Conversely, in the ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 reactions, IC-asc-C9-CoA was converted to IC-asc-C5-CoA, which was partially hydrolyzed to IC-asc-C5 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACOX-1.1 was almost as active towards IC-asc-C7-CoA as it was towards its preferred ascaroside substrate, asc-C9-CoA.
source: ACOX-1.1 was almost as active towards IC-asc-C7-CoA as it was towards its preferred ascaroside substrate, asc-C9-CoA (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOX-1.1 showed activity towards IC-asc-C9-CoA, but less than towards IC-asc-C7-CoA.
source: It also showed activity towards IC-asc-C9-CoA, but less than towards IC-asc-C7-CoA.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ACOX-3 showed low activity towards all substrates tested in the peroxidase-coupled assay.
source: Unfortunately, ACOX-3 showed low activity towards all substrates tested in this assay, including another one of its preferred ascaroside substrates, asc-C13-CoA (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: ACOX-3 may require other β-oxidation enzymes to be fully active.
source: This result may suggest that ACOX-3 requires other β-oxidation enzymes to be fully active (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of low activity in the coupled assay.

claim: ACS-7 has a PTS1-type peroxisomal localization signal.
source: Indeed, ACS-7 has a PTS1-type peroxisomal localization signal.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ACS-7.

claim: ACS-7 was active at neutral pH, but not at the pH found in the lysosome (pH 5.0).
source: Furthermore, when we tested the enzymatic activity of ACS-7, we found that the enzyme was active at neutral pH, but not at the pH found in the lysosome (pH 5.0).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic assays performed at different pH values.

claim: ACS-7, ACOX-3, and ACOX-1.1 are all expressed in a punctate pattern in the intestine.
source: Co-injection of these constructs into wild-type C. elegans showed that all three proteins are expressed in a punctate pattern in the intestine (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The intestinal expression pattern of ACS-7 overlaps with that of ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3.
source: In addition, the intestinal expression pattern of ACS-7 overlaps with that of ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: RNAi against prx-13 leads to a diffuse pattern of expression for ACOX-1.1 and ACS-7 in the intestine.
source: RNAi against prx-13, which is a component of the peroxisomal import machinery (Thieringer et al., 2003), leads to a diffuse pattern of expression for ACOX-1.1 and ACS-7 in the intestine, providing further evidence that these enzymes are localized to the peroxisome (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi data shown in Figure 6C and 6D and citation to previous work.

claim: prx-13 is a component of the peroxisomal import machinery.
source: RNAi against prx-13, which is a component of the peroxisomal import machinery (Thieringer et al., 2003), leads to a diffuse pattern of expression for ACOX-1.1 and ACS-7 in the intestine, providing further evidence that these enzymes are localized to the peroxisome (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ACS-7 likely participates in biosynthesis of the IC-ascarosides in the peroxisome rather than lysosome.
source: Thus, ACS-7 likely participates in biosynthesis of the IC-ascarosides in the peroxisome rather than lysosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data and enzymatic activity at different pH values.

claim: C. elegans can engage in dynamic tailoring of the ascarosides that it has produced.
source: Our data show that C. elegans can engage in dynamic tailoring of the ascarosides that it has produced.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Dynamic tailoring enables C. elegans to respond rapidly to changing environmental conditions and modulate the nature of its chemical message without having to synthesize new ascarosides de novo.
source: This dynamic tailoring enables the worm to respond rapidly to changing environmental conditions and modulate the nature of its chemical message without having to synthesize new ascarosides de novo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: C. elegans attaches the IC head group to ascarosides with medium-length (8–11) side chains to generate aggregation pheromones such as IC-asc-ΔC9 (icas#3).
source: Specifically, we have shown that C. elegans attaches the IC head group to ascarosides with medium-length (8–11) side chains to generate aggregation pheromones such as IC-asc-ΔC9 (icas#3) (Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2 and citation to previous work on biological activity.

claim: C. elegans can activate IC-ascarosides with medium-length side chains for shortening of the side chains through β-oxidation to generate the dauer pheromone IC-asc-C5 (icas#9).
source: We have shown that C. elegans can activate IC-ascarosides with medium-length side chains for shortening of the side chains through β-oxidation to generate the dauer pheromone IC-asc-C5 (icas#9) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by enzymatic and genetic data.

claim: The β-oxidation process that shortens IC-ascarosides likely occurs when environmental conditions become less favorable, such as during starvation.
source: This β-oxidation process likely occurs when environmental conditions become less favorable, such as during starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological context and previous observations.

claim: Starvation conditions have been shown to lead to an increase in the short-chain IC-ascaroside IC-asc-C5 in L1 larvae.
source: Indeed, starvation conditions have been shown to lead to an increase in the short-chain IC-ascaroside IC-asc-C5 in L1 larvae (Artyukhin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bacterial food has been shown to downregulate production of IC-asc-C5 in L4 larvae.
source: Consistent with this result, bacterial food has been shown to downregulate production of IC-asc-C5 in L4 larvae (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Increased production of short-chain IC-ascarosides by starvation conditions would be consistent with their biological role as IC-asc-C5 is a dauer pheromone.
source: Increased production of short-chain IC-ascarosides by starvation conditions would be consistent with their biological role as IC-asc-C5 is a dauer pheromone (Butcher et al., 2009a), and C. elegans would likely want to enter dauer under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological function of IC-asc-C5 and the ecology of C. elegans.

claim: The mechanism allows C. elegans to modulate the balance between aggregation-inducing, medium-chain IC-ascarosides and dauer-inducing, short-chain IC-ascarosides in response to changing environmental conditions.
source: Our work has thus determined the mechanism by which C. elegans modulates the balance between aggregation-inducing, medium-chain IC-ascarosides and dauer-inducing, short-chain IC-ascarosides in response to changing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: The model for biosynthesis of the short-chain IC-ascarosides presented in this study contrasts with the model proposed by Panda et al.
source: Our model for biosynthesis of the short-chain IC-ascarosides, in which β-oxidation of the ascaroside side chain occurs after attachment of the IC head group, contrasts with the model proposed by Panda et al., in which β-oxidation of the ascaroside side chain occurs before attachment of the IC head group (Panda et al., 2017) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current model with the previous model.

claim: ACS-7 activates the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9, as CoA-thioesters, thereby enabling the side chains to be shortened through β-oxidation.
source: We have shown that the acyl-CoA synthetase ACS-7 activates the side chains of medium-chain IC-ascarosides, such as IC-asc-C9, as CoA-thioesters, thereby enabling the side chains to be shortened through β-oxidation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by enzymatic assays.

claim: IC-asc-C9 is a much better substrate for ACS-7 than ICA.
source: Our data show that IC-asc-C9 is a much better substrate for ACS-7, which rapidly converts IC-asc-C9 to the corresponding CoA-thioester, IC-asc-C9-CoA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the enzymatic assay data comparing activity towards IC-asc-C9 and ICA.

claim: Once the side chain of the medium-chain IC-ascarosides is activated, it can be shortened through β-oxidation cycles involving ACOX-1.1, ACOX-3, and likely ACOX-1.4 as well, to make the short-chain IC-ascaroside, IC-asc-C5.
source: We have shown that once the side chain of the medium-chain IC-ascarosides is activated, it can be shortened through β-oxidation cycles involving ACOX-1.1, ACOX-3, and likely ACOX-1.4 as well, to make the short-chain IC-ascaroside, IC-asc-C5.
evidence: This is supported by the mutant analysis and in vitro enzymatic assays.

claim: The acox-1.1;acox-3 double deletion mutant fails to make any IC-asc-C5 and accumulates IC-asc-C7.
source: Specifically, we have shown that the acox-1.1;acox-3 double deletion mutant fails to make any IC-asc-C5 and accumulates IC-asc-C7.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 are able to process IC-asc-C9-CoA to IC-asc-C5-CoA in vitro with the help of the β-oxidation enzymes MAOC-1, DHS-28, and DAF-22.
source: Furthermore, ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3 are able to process IC-asc-C9-CoA to IC-asc-C5-CoA in vitro with the help of the β-oxidation enzymes MAOC-1, DHS-28, and DAF-22.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACS-7, ACOX-1.1, and ACOX-3 appear to be transcriptionally co-regulated.
source: Consistent with ACS-7 working in the same biosynthetic pathway as ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-3, the three genes appear to be transcriptionally co-regulated (von Mering et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on gene co-regulation.

claim: ACOX-3 has been shown to be induced by dietary restriction.
source: ACOX-3 has been shown to be induced by dietary restriction (Palgunow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ACS-7 and ACOX-3 have been shown to be co-regulated by the transcription factor SKN-1.
source: ACS-7 and ACOX-3 have also been shown to be co-regulated by the transcription factor SKN-1, which functions in a variety of stress responses, including detoxification, pathogen defense, the unfolded protein response, and lipid metabolism under starvation conditions (Blackwell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SKN-1 functions in a variety of stress responses, including detoxification, pathogen defense, the unfolded protein response, and lipid metabolism under starvation conditions.
source: ACS-7 and ACOX-3 have also been shown to be co-regulated by the transcription factor SKN-1, which functions in a variety of stress responses, including detoxification, pathogen defense, the unfolded protein response, and lipid metabolism under starvation conditions (Blackwell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ACS-7 is also necessary for biosynthesis of short-chain OS-ascarosides.
source: In addition to the IC-ascarosides, ACS-7 is also necessary for biosynthesis of short-chain OS-ascarosides, as acs-7 mutant worms cannot make the short-chain OS-ascarosides (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ACS-7 likely also activates medium-chain OS-ascarosides for β-oxidation of their side chains.
source: Thus, it is likely that, in addition to medium-chain IC-ascarosides, ACS-7 also activates medium-chain OS-ascarosides for β-oxidation of their side chains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between IC- and OS-ascaroside biosynthesis.

claim: The β-oxidation of IC- and OS-modified ascarosides may be regulated in a similar fashion.
source: The β-oxidation of IC- and OS-modified ascarosides may be regulated in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the similar requirements for ACS-7 in both pathways.

claim: Starvation has been shown to increase the ratio of short-chain (C5) to medium-chain (C9) OS-ascarosides.
source: Starvation has been shown to increase the ratio of short-chain (C5) to medium-chain (C9) OS-ascarosides (Artyukhin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: OS-asc-C5 (osas#9) acts as a dispersal signal that encourages the worm population to seek more favorable conditions.
source: Production of the short-chain OS-ascaroside OS-asc-C5 (osas#9) under starvation conditions is consistent with its biological role, as it acts as a dispersal signal that encourages the worm population to seek more favorable conditions (Artyukhin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The 4'-position of the ascarosides can be modified by the MB and HB head groups.
source: In addition to the IC and OS head groups, the 4'-position of the ascarosides can also be modified by the MB and HB head groups (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MB- and HB-ascarosides with fewer than nine-carbons in their side chains have not been detected in C. elegans.
source: However, MB- and HB-ascarosides with fewer than nine-carbons in their side chains have not been detected in C. elegans (von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Medium-chain MB- and HB-ascarosides probably do not undergo activation by an acyl-CoA synthetase for further β-oxidation in the peroxisome.
source: Thus, unlike medium-chain IC-and OS-ascarosides, medium-chain MB- and HB-ascarosides probably do not undergo activation by an acyl-CoA synthetase for further β-oxidation in the peroxisome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of short-chain MB- and HB-ascarosides.

claim: The lysosome has been shown to be important for biosynthesis of ascarosides modified with a head group on the 4'-position of the ascarylose sugar.
source: The lysosome has been shown to be important for biosynthesis of ascarosides modified with a head group on the 4'-position of the ascarylose sugar (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mutant worms that lack LROs, such as glo-1 mutants, do not make any ascarosides modified on the 4'-position with IC, OS, HB, or MB head groups.
source: Mutant worms that lack LROs, such as glo-1 mutants, do not make any ascarosides modified on the 4'-position with IC, OS, HB, or MB head groups (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Long-chain ascarosides could be shortened to medium- and short-chain ascarosides in the peroxisome, and then medium-chain ascarosides may be transported from the peroxisome to the LROs for attachment of 4'-modifications.
source: In a model that accounts for the role of the LROs in ascaroside biosynthesis, long-chain ascarosides could be shortened to medium- and short-chain ascarosides in the peroxisome, and then medium-chain ascarosides, such as asc-C9, may be transported from the peroxisome to the LROs for attachment of 4'-modifications, such as attachment of the IC head group to make IC-asc-C9, by unknown enzymes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a proposed model that integrates the current findings with previous observations about the role of LROs.

claim: In response to changing internal or external conditions, modified ascarosides could be transported back to the peroxisome for activation by ACS-7 and further β-oxidation of their side chains.
source: In response to changing internal or external conditions, these modified ascarosides could then be transported back to the peroxisome for activation by ACS-7 and further β-oxidation of their side chains (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for dynamic regulation of ascaroside biosynthesis.

claim: Trafficking of the ascarosides through multiple cellular organelles during biosynthesis may enable C. elegans to induce the production of modified ascarosides with specific side-chain lengths only under certain conditions or only in certain tissues.
source: Trafficking of the ascarosides through multiple cellular organelles, such as the peroxisome and LROs, during biosynthesis may enable C. elegans to induce the production of modified ascarosides with specific side-chain lengths only under certain conditions or only in certain tissues.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of organellar trafficking in ascaroside biosynthesis.
